Echocardiography demonstrates a well‑circumscribed 2.8 × 2.6 cm mass in the mid‑apical anteroseptum of the left ventricle and a large pericardial effusion with signs of impending tamponade. ECG shows localized ST‑elevations in V1–V3 (1 mm in V1, 4 mm in V2–V3), T‑wave inversions laterally, and diffuse low voltages. Coronary angiography shows nonobstructive epicardial coronary disease without acute occlusion, and hs‑cTnT is only mildly elevated and unchanged from baseline. Taken together, the imaging and oncologic history make cardiac tumor (metastatic infiltration) with malignant pericardial effusion the most likely cause of the ECG abnormalities and clinical presentation. The normal coronaries, preserved global LV systolic function, absence of regional wall motion abnormality, and chronic/nonrising troponin make an acute occlusive anterior STEMI unlikely. Focal myocarditis, malignant pericarditis, and nonmetastatic intracardiac masses (or thrombus/primary cardiac tumor) are less likely but remain reasonable alternatives.

1. Metastatic myocardial tumor (left ventricular myocardial metastasis from lung cancer) with malignant pericardial involvement causing pericardial effusion/tamponade and tumor‑related localized ST‑elevation (pseudo‑infarct pattern)
2. Malignant pericarditis / malignant pericardial effusion from metastatic lung cancer causing tamponade and ECG low voltages (with secondary ST‑changes)
3. MINOCA (myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries) — anterior necrosis or ischemia (e.g., type 2 MI, distal embolus, or transient occlusion/recanalization) presenting with anterior ST elevation
4. Focal myocarditis (including tumor‑associated inflammatory infiltration of myocardium) producing localized ST elevations and troponin release
5. Primary intracardiac mass or nonmalignant intracardiac lesion (e.g., primary cardiac sarcoma or LV thrombus masquerading as a mass) causing local myocardial injury and ECG changes
